title: Nineteen forty-eight
eyebrow: Four things the family remembers, held against the paper
dek: Told by David on 10 September 2026. Every claim here is lore until a record says otherwise — and on one of them the record already says otherwise.
lead:
This is the first page in this archive built out of **something somebody remembers** rather than something a clerk wrote. It is kept separate for that reason, and graded **lore** throughout.

Lore is not worthless — it is usually the only thing that knows *why*. A register will tell you that a man moved; it will never tell you he was afraid. But lore compresses. Dates slide, two departures become one, and a surname heard in a second language turns into a different surname altogether. So each of the four claims below is set against what this archive already holds, and where they disagree, **the disagreement is the finding**.

claims.against:
**The paper does not allow it, at least not as an emigration.**

Their son was **born at Senj on 17 December 1951**, at 11h50 in the town hospital — this archive holds the certified extract, register 152/1954, page 252, ordinal 110, with the father entered as *Defranceski Ivan, born 25 June 1925 at Crikvenica, electro-mechanic*. And **Ivan died at Senj on 30 October 1995** and is buried there under polished granite cut IVAN DEFRANČESKI.

So in 1951 they were in Senj, and forty-four years later he was still on that coast. Whatever happened in 1948, **it was not a departure from Yugoslavia that stuck.**
readings: **1948 is the marriage.** He was twenty-three, she was twenty-two, and the first child comes in December 1951. A wedding in 1948 fits the arithmetic better than anything else on this page.

**1948 is the move from Crikvenica to Senj.** He was a Crikvenica man; she was a Senj woman; he ended his life in her town and is buried in it. *Going* may mean going twenty-five miles down the coast.
**1948 is a departure that failed or was reversed** — a crossing, a camp, a return. That would leave a paper trail in the refugee files and none in the Yugoslav ones.

**1948 belongs to somebody else in the family.** His brother **Anton** is stamped «Emigré Australie le 8.3.49» and **Zdravko** resettled to Australia in 1949. Two brothers left within a year of 1948, and a family's memory of *when we went* very easily attaches to the wrong pair of names.
claims.settle: The Senj marriage register for 1948, and the Arolsen Archives — which have already given this family the Pfullingen list and Ivan's sickness-fund card, and which would show at once whether either of them was ever in a displaced-persons file.

claims.said: «a post-war migration offering better and safer conditions»
claims.against:
**The year is exactly right for that feeling, and the reasons are not the ones usually assumed.**

This family is **not** part of the Istrian exodus. The Treaty of Paris of February 1947 handed Italian Istria to Yugoslavia and gave its inhabitants the right to opt for Italy; hundreds of thousands took it. But **Crikvenica and Senj were never Italian** — they had been in Croatia since 1918 — so nobody here was an *optant*, and no treaty gave them a door.

What 1948 did give them was fear of a different kind. On **28 June 1948** Yugoslavia was expelled from the Cominform and Tito broke with Stalin, and the purge that followed fell on anyone suspected of siding with Moscow. The camp built for them opened the next year on **Goli otok** — a bare island in the Kvarner, in the water between Senj and Rab. **It is visible from that coast.**

And leaving was not a matter of buying a ticket. Emigration required permission that was rarely given; the practical route out was an illegal crossing into Allied-held Trieste or into Austria, and then a refugee camp and the **International Refugee Organization**, which ran resettlement from 1947 until 1952 and is how both brothers reached Australia.
readings: *inf* — **«better and safer» is two different things and they may have two different dates.** Better points at the shortages and the collectivisation of the late forties. Safer points at 1948 itself, and at the island.
claims.settle: Arolsen Archives and the IRO case files for the surname; the Australian and South African arrival records for the brothers, which would date the family's whole westward movement precisely.

claims.said: «his mother was with another man not that long before, by the last name Carr — and there was always suspicion she perhaps ran away from that as well.»
claims.against:
**«Carr» is almost certainly not an English name.**

On this coast **Car** is a real and ordinary surname — the word means *emperor*, and it is said *tsar*. An English-speaking family in Johannesburg, hearing it and writing it down, produces **Carr** every time. A British Carr in Kvarner in the 1940s would be extraordinary; a Croatian **Car** would be unremarkable, and **the search moves from the wrong country to the right one.**

The woman is **Uršula Kovačina**, born about 1890, married to **Anton Rudolf Defranceski**. And her situation makes the story entirely possible: this archive records Anton Rudolf as having **died in 1943**, which would leave her a widow of about fifty-three with the war still on.

But here the archive has to admit a contradiction of its own, and it is a serious one. **Anton Rudolf stands on the Pfullingen list of foreigners in 1947, and was certified by that town's mayor in 1950.** He cannot be both dead in 1943 and certified in 1950. One of those two facts is about a different man, or the 1943 death — which is held only «per the family», itself lore — is wrong.

**Until that is resolved, this archive does not know whether Uršula was a widow or a wife.** Which is precisely the question the story turns on.
readings: *inf* — if the 1943 death is right, a second partnership by 1947–48 needs no explanation at all beyond ordinary life.
*inf* — if Anton Rudolf was alive in 1950, then «with another man» means something else entirely, and the word **ran** in the family's telling starts to carry weight.
claims.settle: The Crikvenica or Senj death register for 1943; the Pfullingen certificate of 1950, which this archive holds as a plate and has not fully read; and then the registers for the surname **Car** in Crikvenica, Senj and Novi Vinodolski.

claims.against:
**This one the archive can do nothing but believe, and it explains something it could not explain before.**

Hedviga Blažević was a **Senj** woman — born there, daughter of Ljubomir Blažević and Milka Papić the tobacco-factory cigar-roller, out of a line of Senj carriers reaching back past 1768. Ivan was a **Crikvenica** man. Twenty-five miles of coast road lie between the two towns, and nothing in this archive has ever explained how they met.

**Singing in Crikvenica explains it.** Crikvenica was not a village but a **climatic health resort** — hotels, a season, a promenade, an orchestra, visitors from Vienna and Budapest and then from all over Yugoslavia. A singer worked where the season was, and the season was there and not at Senj. A Senj girl with a voice went **to** Crikvenica to use it, and met a Crikvenica boy who had come home from a Reutlingen factory floor at seventeen.

It is the only detail on this page that is purely a gift. It adds a **profession** to a woman this archive had recorded only as a wife, a mother and a date of death.

transposition.heading: And one thing nobody said, which the archive found while checking
transposition.text:
Hedviga's date of birth is in this project **twice, and the two do not agree**.

The Crikvenica and Senj pages both give **8 March 1926**. The certified extract from the Senj birth register — the one attached to her son's 1951 birth entry and translated for the Supreme Court of South Africa — gives **3 August 1926**.

Read them as numbers and the fault is obvious: **8/3/1926 and 3/8/1926**. A day and a month have changed places, almost certainly when a European date met an English-speaking clerk or a translator working the other way.

This archive does not know which is right and **will not pick the one it likes**. It is one line of the Senj birth register for 1926, and it is now an errand.

close:
None of the four claims is discarded and none is promoted. What has changed is that they are **written down, dated, attributed and answerable** — and that two of them have already forced the archive to look at itself: a man recorded as dying in 1943 who is certified alive in 1950, and a woman with two birthdays that are the same numbers in the wrong order.

That is what oral history is for. It does not settle anything. **It tells you where to look, and it tells you what the paper never will** — that somebody, at some point, was frightened enough to leave.
source: Told by David Defranceski, 10 September 2026, and recorded the same day. Held against: the certified extract of the Senj birth register 152/1954; the Crikvenica register entries and family file on the Crikvenica house; the Senj and Karlobag material on the Senj line; the Arolsen Archives Pfullingen list and sickness-fund card; and the gravestone at Senj. Historical background: the Cominform expulsion of 28 June 1948, the Treaty of Paris of 10 February 1947, and the International Refugee Organization, 1947–1952.
